M0C-01-INDEXMATCH.14:
## Why you don't use VLOOKUP

Below is this year's customer revenue list for the {p0} customers, with each one's annual revenue.
You need the revenue of one specific customer: **{clienteCercato}**, written in {celQuery}.

`VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table, column_index, 0)` works by finding the name in the first
column and taking the value from column number `column_index` — a fixed number, counted by hand.
The problem comes the day someone inserts a column in the middle of the table (`Sector`,
`Region`, anything): the table shifts, but that index stays the same number. VLOOKUP keeps
taking the wrong column, with no error on screen — the sheet seems to work and lies.
That's how a model produces the wrong number in a meeting, with everyone convinced it's right.

`MATCH(lookup_value, list, 0)` solves only half the problem: it finds **the position** of the name
within its list (the third argument set to 0 requires an exact match, not an approximate one).
`INDEX(range, position)` takes the value at that position within **another range**.

Together, `INDEX(value_range, MATCH(name, name_range, 0))` never counts columns:
if a column is inserted in the middle, both the name range and the value range move
with it, and the formula stays correct without you touching it.
M0C-01-INDEXMATCH.20: MATCH({celQuery}, {colNomi}:A{dataEnd}, 0). The final zero means "exact match only".
M0C-01-INDEXMATCH.21: MATCH's result is the position WITHIN the list, not the sheet row: if the customer is third in the table, MATCH returns 3 even if that row is number 6.
M0C-01-INDEXMATCH.22: INDEX({colValori}:B{dataEnd}, MATCH({celQuery}, {colNomi}:A{dataEnd}, 0)): paste inside INDEX the same MATCH you already wrote in {celMatch}.
M0C-01-INDEXMATCH.23: If the result is #N/A, the name you're looking for isn't written exactly as in the table: case and spaces don't matter, but a different character does.
M0C-01-INDEXMATCH.title: Look up by name, not by index

M0C-02-MATCHTIPO.16:
## The third argument nobody looks at

`MATCH(lookup_value, array, match_type)` has a third argument that almost
everyone forgets. It's not a detail: it radically changes how it searches.

- **0** = exact match. Finds that precise value, wherever it is, in whatever order
  the list is. If it can't find it, `#N/A`.
- **1** (the default if you omit it) = approximate match. Assumes the list is
  sorted **ascending** and returns the largest value less than or equal to the one searched for.

Below are the desk's last {p0} mandates, logged in the order they
arrived — not by ID. On a list like that, an approximate match raises no error:
it still returns a row, with a number in it, and that number looks real. You find out
it's wrong only when someone checks the total against the original invoice — months later,
in a meeting, with the wrong client on your lips.

The opposite case is the second table: margin brackets by entry leverage, from
{p1} upwards. Here ascending order is guaranteed, and it's REALLY needed: the actual leverage
of a deal almost never matches a table threshold exactly, so the exact match
would always give `#N/A`. The approximate match isn't a fallback here: it's the right
tool to find "which bracket I fall into".

The difference between the two isn't the formula — it's whether the list underneath is sorted or not.
Look at it before writing MATCH, not after the number is already wrong.

M0C-02-MATCHTIPO.28: If you leave the third argument empty, Excel assumes 1: on a list sorted by date and not by ID the result is another mandate, with a number that looks real.
M0C-02-MATCHTIPO.29: INDEX(B17:B21, MATCH(B23, A17:A21, 1)): here the third argument is 1 (or you can omit it) because the minimum-leverage column is sorted ascending — the only case where that's fine.
M0C-02-MATCHTIPO.title: MATCH: exact or approximate?

M0C-03-SUMIFS.20:
## One criterion is almost never enough

Below is the sales log for the first quarter: {p0} transactions, each with
a customer, a product category, a month and an amount.

`SUMIF` (without the S) can add on **one** criterion. In practice almost every question you'll
get has two or three at once: "how much of this category did we sell in March" isn't
one question, it's two crossed questions. With one criterion you get a number that looks
right and isn't: the category alone includes the other months, the month alone includes the
other categories.

`SUMIFS`, `COUNTIFS` and `MAXIFS` take as many criteria as you need, and the form is always
the same: first (if needed) the range to aggregate, then the **range-criterion** pairs
one after the other — as many as you want. `COUNTIFS` is the exception on just one point: there's nothing
to add, so there's no first range, you start straight from the pairs.

The three queries below ask you for the three functions on the same kind of crossing.
The first query's total, to give you an idea of the order of magnitude, is close to
{p1}.
M0C-03-SUMIFS.26: SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criterion1, criteria_range2, criterion2). The first argument is what to add ({rifImporti} downwards), then the pairs follow.
M0C-03-SUMIFS.27: COUNTIFS has ONLY range-criterion pairs: no range to add up front, you start straight from the first pair.
M0C-03-SUMIFS.28: MAXIFS has the same form as SUMIFS: the range to search for the maximum, then the range-criterion pairs.
M0C-03-SUMIFS.title: Two criteria, not one: SUMIFS and family

M0C-04-SUMPRODUCT.16:
## The product of two columns, without a third

You're doing commercial due diligence on a target company. The month's sales log lists
{p0} product lines, with the units sold and the average price per unit for each.

**Total revenue** is the sum of quantity times price, row by row. You could write
a column E with `=C4*D4` copied down, then add it up: it works, but it leaves in the model
a column nobody will ever ask you to see in a report. **`SUMPRODUCT`** does the
same thing in one go: it multiplies two ranges element by element and adds up the
results, without leaning on anything else.

`SUMPRODUCT(quantities, prices)` — two ranges of the same shape, separated by a comma.

SUMPRODUCT, though, has a second job, less obvious than the first: it can **count**. A comparison
like `B4:B13="Retail"` doesn't return a number: it returns an array of TRUE and FALSE, one
per row. Multiplying it by `1` turns it into an array of 1s and 0s. Adding up that array —
that is, `SUMPRODUCT((B4:B13="Retail")*1)` — gives exactly the number of rows that meet
the condition: the same result as `COUNTIF(B4:B13,"Retail")`, but built from the same
bricks — array, product, sum — you just used for revenue.
M0C-04-SUMPRODUCT.23: SUMPRODUCT({rangeQuantita},{rangePrezzi}): multiplies each quantity row by the matching price row and adds everything up, no extra column needed.
M0C-04-SUMPRODUCT.24: SUMPRODUCT(({rangeCanali}="{canaleTarget}")*1): the comparison gives TRUE/FALSE for each row, the *1 turns it into 1/0, SUMPRODUCT adds up that array.
M0C-04-SUMPRODUCT.25: {p0} is the expected revenue: if your number is different, check that you took the same {p1} rows for both ranges.
M0C-04-SUMPRODUCT.title: One product per row, a single sum

M0C-05-OFFSET.14:
## OFFSET: the value that moves from a fixed point

You have the monthly revenue of {filiale}, for the last {periodi} months: from Month 1 (the
oldest) to Month {periodi} (the most recent). The latter, in {ancoraRef}, is your
**anchor**: the fixed point you count backwards from.

`OFFSET(reference, rows, cols)` doesn't search for a value like INDEX/MATCH: it **moves**,
literally, by a certain number of rows and columns from the reference you give it.
Positive rows go down, negative rows go up; positive columns go right, negative ones
left. To go back in time along a column, the number of rows must be
negative.

The number of months to count back must not be written inside the formula: it's already in
{paramNRef}. Read it from there, with the minus sign in front — that's the difference between a formula
that works only for this case and one that also works the day that number
changes. In a real model it changes often.

A technical note, not just praise for the function: OFFSET is **volatile**. Excel recalculates it on
every change to the sheet, even when none of its arguments changed. On a table
as small as this nobody notices; on a model with hundreds of OFFSETs it's
often the first cause when recalculation starts to slow down. Use it when you really
need a reference that moves, not as an automatic substitute for INDEX/MATCH.

M0C-06-CHOOSE.6:
## One index, many options

`IF` chooses between two answers. But a real model rarely lives on just two scenarios:
usually there are three — conservative, base, ambitious — and sometimes more. Nesting `IF` inside
`IF` to get there works, but quickly becomes unreadable and fragile with every scenario
added.

**`CHOOSE(index, option1, option2, option3, ...)`** returns the option in the
position given by `index` — 1 returns the first, 2 the second, and so on.
A single number, the index, drives which scenario is "on" across the whole model: change it
and every cell that uses CHOOSE updates by itself, without touching the formulas.

In this instance the scenario index is **{p0}** ({p1}).
The three starting revenues are {p2} (Conservative), {p3} (Base) and
{p4} (Ambitious); the three growth assumptions for the following year are
{p5}, {p6} and {p7}.

In the second task the difference from the first is precise: you're no longer choosing among three
ready-made numbers, but among three FORMULAS — each one is the calculation that holds if that's the
right scenario. That's how CHOOSE stops being a shortcut for IF and becomes the
building block of the scenario switch: the same structure that, later on, will drive a whole
valuation model with a single number to change.
